clay — Clay is plastic when wet and becomes hard ceramic when fired.
wood — Wood carving removes pieces of timber with cutting tools to create a form.

water lilies — The Water Lilies series studies the reflections, plants and changing light of the garden pond.
sunflowers — Van Gogh painted several famous still lifes of sunflowers in vases.
still life — A still life uses arranged inanimate objects as its main subject.
photograph — A photograph records light from a scene using a camera.
the Mona Lisa — The Mona Lisa’s subtly modelled expression is one reason the portrait became so celebrated.
cave painting — Cave paintings preserve animals, signs and human activity on the walls and ceilings of prehistoric caves.
Michelangelo — Michelangelo painted the vast Sistine Chapel ceiling frescoes in the early 16th century.

the Mona Lisa — La Gioconda is the Italian title commonly used for the Mona Lisa.

graffiti — Graffiti ranges from quick signatures called tags to elaborate painted pieces.
a stencil — Paint passes through the open areas of a stencil, reproducing the planned design.
a mural — A mural is designed as part of an architectural surface rather than as a movable framed picture.

a rotunda — A rotunda is defined by its circular plan; the Pantheon’s main interior is a famous example.

the pointed arch — The pointed arch directs forces efficiently and gives Gothic interiors their strong vertical lines.

stained glass — Medieval stained-glass windows assembled coloured pieces with lead strips to tell sacred stories.

a rose window — Rose windows arrange stone tracery and coloured glass radially like the petals of a flower.
nature — Designers drew organic ornament from plants and animals, rejecting simple copies of older historical styles.

Kaunas — Kaunas expanded rapidly as Lithuania’s temporary capital, leaving a coherent legacy of interwar modern architecture.

porcelain — Porcelain is fired at high temperature and traditionally uses materials including kaolin.
terracotta — Iron in the clay commonly gives terracotta its warm orange-red colour after firing.
glaze — Glaze ingredients melt during firing and fuse into a glass-like layer on the clay body.
a kiln — A kiln holds the controlled high temperatures needed to harden clay and mature ceramic glazes.

embroidery — Embroidery adds stitched motifs to an existing fabric using many possible threads and techniques.

batik — Batik alternates wax resist and dye baths to build layered patterns on cloth.
macramé — Macramé forms patterns through knots rather than weaving on a loom or knitting with needles.

engraving — In engraving, ink held in the incised metal lines prints under strong pressure.

lithography — Lithography is planographic: the printing and non-printing areas remain on the same flat surface.
screen printing — A separate mesh stencil controls each colour in a screen-printed image.
a logo — A logo gives an organisation a recognisable visual identity across signs, products and media.
typography — Typography shapes how written language looks and guides a reader through a design.
a poster — Posters are designed to communicate a message quickly at a distance through bold image and type.
a pictogram — Pictograms use recognisable visual forms so information can cross language boundaries.
negative space — Negative space is an active part of composition and can even form a hidden secondary image.

impasto — The Italian-derived term describes paint thick enough to stand out from the canvas; oil and heavy-body acrylic are common media.
